title: 3 Simple Ways To Earn Your Students' Respect https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/10/13/3-simple-ways-to-earn-your-students-respect/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that respect can't be taught through lectures or role-play; it must be earned, and students are actively looking for a leader worthy of it. He lays out three keys: keeping your word golden by always following through, being emotionally consistent day to day rather than moody or unpredictable, and never taking misbehavior personally so consequences are enforced matter-of-factly. Each behavior, he explains, builds trust and removes the friction that comes from inconsistency or perceived unfairness. He notes that letting a classroom management plan handle accountability preserves the teacher's warm, positive persona while still holding firm standards. The piece closes by describing respect as something earned through quiet strength rather than a commanding personality or forceful demands.
points: Respect can't be taught or demanded — it must be earned through consistent, trustworthy behavior.
A teacher's word must be reliably followed through, since broken promises are the single greatest cause of student disrespect.
Being emotionally the same teacher every day, rather than moody or unpredictable, builds the trust needed for rapport.
Never taking misbehavior personally allows consequences to be enforced matter-of-factly, avoiding the friction of backtalk or challenge.
Respect is earned through the honor of your word, steadiness of temperament, and quiet strength, not through a dominant personality.
quotes: But in the end, students can’t be persuaded or talked into respecting you. No, in this day and age, respect must be earned.
If you say it, you must follow through with it. Saying one thing and doing another is the single greatest reason why teachers struggle with disrespect.
Your students won’t respect you if you’re moody and unpredictable. Snapping at them one day and behaving as sweet as summer squash on another is confusing and disorienting to students.

When you allow students to get under your skin, it’s hard not to fall into hurtful methods like yelling, lecturing, arguing, and sarcasm—which in turn causes students to view you as a peer-equal they can backtalk, challenge, and wrest control from.
Sadly, you can no longer expect students to arrive in your classroom with a healthy respect for teachers already impressed upon their heart.
Respect is earned through the honor of your word, the steadiness of your temperament, and the gentle, quiet strength of your convictions.
